## Homework review: Christmas gift

::: {.teaching-file}
[Homework solution]{.teaching-label .teaching-label-homework} [`../materials/exercises_with_solutions.xlsx`](../materials/exercises_with_solutions.xlsx){.teaching-button .teaching-button-homework} -- Sheet: Gift
:::

Students should retrieve two values based on customer status:

- Christmas gift
- Packaging

The values come from two different lookup tables.

### `VLOOKUP` solution

Review:

- The lookup value is the customer status.
- The lookup column must be the first column of the selected table.
- The return-column number is 2.
- Use `FALSE` for an exact match.
- Lock the lookup ranges before copying the formulas.

![](../images/excel_gift_vlookup.png){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

### `XLOOKUP` solution

Copy the sheet before creating the `XLOOKUP` solution.

Contrast the formula structure with `VLOOKUP`:

```text
=XLOOKUP(lookup_value,lookup_array,return_array)
```

![](../images/excel_xlookup.png){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## Slides 54–60 — Pivot tables: From data to management questions

::: {.teaching-file}
[In-class demo]{.teaching-label .teaching-label-demo} [`../materials/exercises.xlsx`](../materials/exercises.xlsx){.teaching-button .teaching-button-demo} -- Sheets: Sales_data | Sales_pivot
:::

Refer to the Excel Table example (from previous session): highlight that manually writing formulas for aggregate and conditional statistics can be tedious (e.g., by product, region, time).
PivotTables help for that.

### Slide 65 — Creating a PivotTable

Before creating the PivotTable, briefly check that:

- Each column has one header.
- Each row represents one observation.
- There are no blank header cells.
- Numerical facts are stored as numbers.
- Dates are stored as actual Excel dates.

Demonstrate the process in Excel: Select source dataset > choose **Insert → PivotTable**

Remember to explicitly refresh the data through the ribbon.

::: {.callout-tip titl="Pro tip"}
Insert an Excel Table first, then Insert a PivotTable (PivotTables could be created without an Excel Table, but the references are much clearer with object names)
:::

### Example: Build the reports from the slides step by step

Key message:

> A PivotTable makes it possible to generate different analytical views from the same underlying records without manually constructing each summary table.

Begin with the decisions and questions that the data should support (instead of the mechanics of PivotTables).

Ask students to modify one field at a time and predict the resulting table before releasing the mouse button.

Show that the same sales data can answer different questions by creating pivot tables for the following:

### What is total turnover in 2020?

- Filter for `year = 2020`
- Values: `Sum of turnover`
- Filter for `category`, use `actual`

Demonstrate two kinds of filters:

- Report filters above the PivotTable
- Filters attached to row or column labels

For demonstration: Filter the product columns to retain only selected products.

Emphasize:

- Filtering changes the displayed slice.
- It does not delete the underlying observations.
- Grand totals are recalculated based on the active filter.

### What is turnover by product group in 2020?

- Drag `product` to rows

### What is turnover in the first three months of 2020?

- Drag `month` to columns
- Filter for first three months

### What is turnover by region in the first three months of 2020?

- Remove `product` from rows
- Drag `region` to rows

### What is the turnover in each region by product group in 2019 and 2020?

- Columns: Remove `month`, add `product`
- Rows: `region`, then `year`
- Filter: `year`, for 2019 and 2020.

### How can we show turnover as a percentage of total?

- Right-click, `Show values as`, **try and interpret different options**
- Undo
- Select the right-click, `Value Field Settings', show option to display averages, ...

Distinguish carefully between:

- The numerical aggregation used to create a value
- The way the resulting value is displayed

For example:

- Aggregation: `Sum`
- Display: `% of Grand Total`

Explain a common error: When Excel interprets a numerical column as text, it may use `Count` instead of `Sum`.

### How do actual and target values compare?

- Drag `category` to columns
- Remove filter for `category`

### How can (sub)totals be modified?

Through `Design` ribbon:

- Subtotals
- Grand totals (e.g., Off for rows and columns).

::: {.callout-tip title="Summary"}
- Creating a PivotTable
- Selecting columns/rows (first/second/third... order)
- Filtering to select values
- Changing Values (Sum, Percentage, ....)
- Values selection: can include different attributes (e.g., cost and turnover) or differnt aggregations of the same attribute (e.g., sum and average of turnover)
:::

::: {.teaching-break}
Break — 10 minutes
:::

### Slide 73 — PivotCharts

Create a PivotChart from the current PivotTable.

Demonstrate that:

- The chart is connected to the PivotTable.
- PivotTable filters also change the chart.
- Fields can be filtered directly through the chart controls.

<!-- **SCREENSHOT:** PivotChart with visible field controls. -->

### Slide 74 — Calculated fields

**PivotTable Analyze → Fields, Items & Sets → Calculated Field**

Create a calculated field:

```text
Name: Profit
Formula: =Turnover-Cost
```

Add the calculated field and use it in the Values area.

Key point:

> Calculated fields refer to source-field names rather than worksheet cells.

<!-- **SCREENSHOT:** Calculated Field dialog with the `Profit` formula. -->

### Slide 75 — Grouping dates

**Important**: Create PivotTable for the `Store_data` sheet, which contains dates!

::: {.teaching-file}
[In-class demo]{.teaching-label .teaching-label-demo} [`../materials/exercises.xlsx`](../materials/exercises.xlsx){.teaching-button .teaching-button-demo} -- Sheets: Store_data | Store_pivot
:::

Explain that PivotTables can aggregate an actual date field automatically.

Demonstrate:

1. Place the date field in **Rows**.
2. Observe auto-grouping (years/quarters/months)
3. Highlight that the original data is more granular
4. Right-click one of the dates.
6. Select **Group**.
7. Unselect `Months`, `Quarters`, and `Years`. Select `Days`.

## Theory : Data warehouse concepts, including data cubes and facts vs dimensions


Typically, there are some attributes that we will use for the `values` and others that will be used for `rows`, `columns` and `filters`.
For `values`, we need data that can be aggregated numerically (e.g., through sum functions), for the others, we prefer categorical data that allows us to group observations.
These we refer to as facts and dimensions.
This corresponds to the multi-dimensional hypercube analyses in Excel (a type of analysis that we will also see in other analytical software packages).

### Slide 61 — Facts and dimensions

Introduce the distinction using the table on the slide.

| Type       | Purpose                                   | Examples                               |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Dimensions | Describe, classify, group, or filter data | Region, product, category, month, year |
| Facts      | Numerical values that can be aggregated   | Turnover, cost, profit, quantity       |

Revisit Slides 56–61. Select two or three examples and ask students:

- Which number is being aggregated?
- Which categories are used to divide the number?
- Which values are fixed or filtered?

### Slides 62–63 — Data cube and slicing

Use the cube as a conceptual model.
Explain:

- Each dimension provides a perspective on the data.
- A fact is stored for combinations of dimension values.
- A PivotTable therefore presents a two-dimensional slice of a multidimensional dataset.
- Filters fix the dimensions that are not currently shown in rows or columns.

## Slide 78 — Exercise: Expeditioner pivot analysis

::: {.teaching-file}
[In-class exercise]{.teaching-label .teaching-label-exercise}/[Homework]{.teaching-label .teaching-label-homework} [`../materials/exercises.xlsx`](../materials/exercises.xlsx){.teaching-button .teaching-button-exercise} -- Sheets: Exped_data | Exped_pivot
:::

**Note**: Sales refers to the **REVENUE** column (unless we refer to the number of products).

- Briefly inspect the dataset and available attributes.
- Reproduce the report shown on the slide:

![](../images/excel_pivot_exped_start.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

### Question 1 — London catalog sales in Q1

![](../images/excel_pivot_exped_1.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

- Move `WHEN` from **Filters** to **Rows** so the dates can be grouped and compared.
- Move `WHERE` from **Rows** to **Filters**, then filter it to London.
- Right-click a date (or select a date and choose **Group Selection**), choose **Group**, select **Quarters**, and deselect **Months** if necessary.
- In the `HOW` column field, show Catalog only. Read the Catalog value for Qtr1.

### Question 2 — Tokyo Q4 Web sales as a percentage of annual sales

![](../images/excel_pivot_exped_2.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

- Filter `WHERE` to Tokyo.
- Keep `HOW` in **Columns**, grouped `WHEN` / Quarters in **Rows**, and `REVENUE` in **Values**.
- Open **Value Field Settings**, choose **Show Values As**, and select **% of Grand Total**. This makes every cell a share of Tokyo's annual total across all channels.
- Read the Web value for Qtr4.

### Question 3 — Sydney annual Catalog share

![](../images/excel_pivot_exped_3.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

- Filter `WHERE` to Sydney.
- Keep `HOW` in **Columns**, grouped `WHEN` / Quarters in **Rows**, and `REVENUE` in **Values**.
- In **Value Field Settings** > **Show Values As**, select **% of Grand Total**.
- Use the **Grand Total** row in the Catalog column; this combines all quarters and therefore gives the annual Catalog share.

### Question 4 — Camel saddle sales for Paris by quarter

![](../images/excel_pivot_exped_4.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

- Filter `WHAT` to Camel saddle and `WHERE` to Paris.
- Put grouped `WHEN` / Quarters in **Rows**, keep `HOW` in **Columns**, and keep `REVENUE` in **Values** as **Sum of REVENUE**.
- Read each quarter from the **Grand Total** column, which adds the sales channels for that quarter.

### Question 5 — London January Catalog sales and source transactions

![](../images/excel_pivot_exped_5.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

- Filter `WHERE` to London and restrict `HOW` to Catalog.
- Change the `WHEN` date grouping from Quarters to **Months**, then read the January value.

::: {.callout-tip title="Inspecting results"}
- To inspect the contributing records, double-click `411` (or use **Show Details**). Excel creates a new worksheet containing the source records behind that PivotTable cell.
- The two records are:

![](../images/excel_pivot_exped_5_detail.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

- Check that `275 + 136 = 411`.
:::

### Question 6 — Elephant polo stick quantities in New York by month

![](../images/excel_pivot_exped_6.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

- Filter `WHAT` to Elephant polo stick and `WHERE` to New York.
- Group `WHEN` by **Months** in **Rows**.
- Remove `REVENUE` from **Values**, add `QUANTITY`, and confirm that the calculation is **Sum of QUANTITY**. This reports units sold rather than sales value.
- Read the quantities for the months displayed in the PivotTable; do not infer values for months that are absent.
